1.1.explanation: Translating a business problem starts with the business outcome, not the model, and traces the full shape: users, inputs, data boundaries, processing stages, outputs, feedback, and the metric that proves value. The core discipline is splitting the work three ways — what suits language understanding, planning, drafting, or tool-mediated action; what an existing system already does reliably; and what a person must retain. Over-assigning to the model is the most expensive early mistake because it is also the easiest to defend in a demo.
1.1.example: A support organization asks for faster resolution. The translation yields a classifier that routes tickets, retrieval over the knowledge base for draft answers, a deterministic refund rule kept in the billing system, and a human step for escalations — with average resolution time as the tracked metric.
1.1.guidance: Justify every model assignment on three questions: can a wrong call be undone, what does a wrong call cost, and who answers for it. The classic error is handing a threshold that must hold on every case to a system that holds on most — it fails on the untidy inputs nobody tested and surfaces in an audit rather than in monitoring.

1.2.explanation: An end-to-end architecture traces one request through ingestion, model calls, tools, validation, delivery, and feedback, with every boundary annotated for trust level, failure mode, fallback, and owner. The feedback loop closes the system: outputs are measured in production and the results flow back into prompts, retrieval, and the evaluation set.
1.2.example: A document pipeline ingests PDFs, extracts fields with Claude, validates against schema and confidence thresholds, routes low-confidence extractions to reviewers, and feeds corrections back as labeled evaluation cases.
1.2.guidance: Draw the request path end to end before choosing components — an architecture that cannot say where a request dies is not yet a design. Boundary annotations are the deliverable: trust level, failure mode, fallback, owner, observable signal.

1.3.explanation: Three shapes sit on one spectrum: a single augmented LLM call, a workflow whose control flow lives in your code, and an agent whose control flow lives inside the model. Five factors decide in order — predictability, error cost, observability, latency budget, and cost — and the first factor that rules a shape out decides. Within workflows, chain stages that consume each other's output, route inputs that differ in kind, parallelize genuinely independent work, and add generate-then-critique only when quality is verifiable.
1.3.example: A compliant summarization of fixed inputs is a chain with deterministic guards between steps; an open-ended research task with no enumerable path justifies an agent bounded by its toolset and a turn limit.
1.3.guidance: Eliminate by constraint, not preference — enumerate the steps if you can, and prefer the workflow whose guards you wrote. Choosing an agent because the work feels open-ended is not the same as being unable to write the steps down; teams that mine traces often find a router and a few chains rebuilt expensively inside a loop.

1.4.explanation: A coordinator owns the goal, decomposes work, and synthesizes; workers each carry one scoped unit in their own context. Failures are asymmetric: a malformed or missing worker result is recoverable at the worker boundary, disagreement between workers is recoverable at synthesis with a tie-breaking rule, but a coordinator that loses the goal or its merge state usually loses the run.
1.4.example: An audit orchestrator splits a repository into per-directory workers, checks that completed units match dispatched units before summarizing, applies an explicit rule when two workers disagree, and checkpoints its own merge state so a failed run resumes instead of restarting.
1.4.guidance: Reach for multi-agent only when work genuinely exceeds one context — every added agent is another boundary to observe and govern. The dangerous failure is silent: reconcile coverage at synthesis so a fluent summary cannot hide missing work, and propagate one trace identifier so a run reconstructs end to end.

1.5.explanation: Decomposition splits a complex task into bounded components with explicit contracts and ownership, and it comes before architecture: the split is work that suits the model, work existing systems already do reliably, and work a person must retain. Each component needs an input, an output, and a failure you can name.
1.5.example: A contract-analysis request decomposes into clause extraction, comparison against a playbook, and exception review — each component independently testable, so a failure localizes to one contract instead of the whole request.
1.5.guidance: Split until every component has a contract you can test and an owner who answers for it. Where a subtask cannot be bounded, that is the signal for a human step or a narrower problem statement — not a bigger prompt.

1.6.explanation: Value pillars — efficiency, transformation, productivity, solution cost, and performance service levels — are the language the budget holder shares with the blueprint. The case is a comparison: the baseline measured in a unit the business already tracks, the projection in the same unit, minus run cost from your own sizing model, expressed as a payback period with sensitivity. Feasibility is a verdict plus the constraint that makes it true — feasible as scoped, feasible under stated constraints, or not feasible, with the boundary condition named.
1.6.example: An automation case compares measured handle time with the projected state, states that reviewers still handle part of the volume, and presents payback under best- and worst-case ticket mixes.
1.6.guidance: Three errors recur: a baseline estimated rather than measured, a projection that models full automation while the design still routes work to reviewers, and run cost taken from an average when the input distribution has a heavy tail. An undocumented constraint becomes an infeasible system the moment production violates it.

2.1.explanation: Model choice matches capability, speed, and cost to each unit of work instead of defaulting every stage to one tier. Start at the balanced tier and move on evaluation evidence: up when the default misses the quality bar, down when the eval confirms the drop is acceptable for that task. Per-step routing only becomes possible when per-step evaluations exist.
2.1.example: A pipeline keeps a balanced tier everywhere until the evaluation shows extraction missing the bar on one category — then routes that category to a stronger model and leaves the rest alone.
2.1.guidance: Treat a model swap as a release: a curated case set covering the real work distribution, a grading function, and a rollback threshold agreed before the run. Results broken out by input type often expose a partial migration one averaged number conceals — send the regressed classes up and route the rest down.

2.2.explanation: A reused prompt is an asset with structure: a stated role and scope, the constraints that must hold, and an output contract naming the response shape. The skill worth practicing is spotting what a prompt leaves unsaid — wherever it is silent, the model improvises, differently each time. A well-built template makes the guarded path the path of least resistance.
2.2.example: A support-drafting template fixes the section structure, embeds the prohibited-claims rule as a required property of the output contract, and leaves only the ticket body as a filled slot — the scaffolding carries the guarantee, so filling a slot cannot remove it.
2.2.guidance: Express must-hold rules as structural requirements of the output rather than one more line of role description, because a guardrail written as prose can be drifted past. Review templates for silence: constraints nobody wrote are constraints nobody enforced.

2.3.explanation: Use the lightest technique that clears the bar: instruction alone first, examples when showing the desired shape is easier than specifying it, and explicit step-by-step reasoning only when the reasoning path genuinely determines the answer — each escalation costs tokens and latency on every call. Identical wording does not produce identical behavior across tiers or generations, so a prompt tuned on one model is a draft for the next.
2.3.example: A structured extraction passes zero-shot with a schema; an unusual output casing is pinned with one example instead of a paragraph of description; a multi-step reconciliation gets explicit reasoning because the path determines the result.
2.3.guidance: Watch for bias introduced by construction — leading phrasing, an example set drawn from one kind of case, instructions that presume the answer. No single output reveals that skew; it shows up only across many, which is what the evaluation set is for.

2.4.explanation: Four context mechanisms stay distinct: the window itself (active attention, resets between calls), retrieval (fetches external knowledge at query time), application state (lives in your systems, reached by tool call), and memory or summaries (continuity your application stores and passes back). Four delivery strategies layer in production — load everything, carry recent state, fetch just in time, compact into summaries — and each breaks differently: attention degrades before the hard limit, dropped detail breaks later turns, missed retrieval breaks synthesis, and summaries drop load-bearing identifiers one-way.
2.4.example: A long-running analyst session carries recent turns, retrieves policy documents on demand, keeps account state behind a tool, and compacts everything older than the current task into a summary that preserves open decisions.
2.4.guidance: Size the window for the largest conversation you actually expect, then add system prompt, retrieval, and headroom — the window is a ceiling, not a target. Ask four separate questions: what the model needs at the start, from recent steps, on demand, and what compresses without losing decision-relevant detail.

2.5.explanation: Prompt caching saves on an unchanging prefix that is identical byte for byte across requests, so stable content goes first and per-request content last — ordering is the mechanism, not configuration. Extended reasoning is a measured decision: it bills tokens and adds latency on every call where it is engaged, so run the evaluation without it and enable it only where a measured gap justifies the cost. Reuse across a team is a governance choice between a shared library, versioned self-contained packages, and ungoverned copying.
2.5.example: A pipeline places its long policy preamble and tool schemas before the cache breakpoint and the user's document last, so the prefix caches; engaging reasoning on the routing classifier is declined because the evaluation shows no gap.
2.5.guidance: Cache only content that holds still — where the cached content must reflect live state, the consistency window can disqualify it. Prefer versioned packages for stable procedures that travel across teams, and expect ungoverned copies to drift into slightly different behaviors.

3.1.explanation: Capability bloat is a tool set grown past what the task needs: every tool costs tokens on every request, degrades selection accuracy as the catalog grows, and enlarges the space of actions never tested. Tools are audited the way permissions are audited — with the reason each removal was safe recorded. Protocol habits fail both ways: a shared protocol layer with one client buys integration cost and no reuse, and a developer-facing surface in front of non-developers ships friction nobody asked for.
3.1.example: An agent configured with twelve tools misroutes calls; the audit shows four unused since launch and two overlapping, and removing them restores selection accuracy while shrinking the prompt.
3.1.guidance: Remove tools an agent does not need instead of relying on instructions or confirmations to steer around them. Recognize the integration carried forward out of habit from the last project — that is the failure the exam is pointing at.

3.2.explanation: Five layers decide whether an enterprise integration survives review: compliance (which routes remain permitted once the obligation applies), identity (where authentication happens relative to the model call), authorization (which capabilities and data this role may reach), data handling (which fields genuinely need to enter the context), and observability (what you must reconstruct afterwards). A user asserting a role inside their own message is not identity — identity is injected by the server after authentication.
3.2.example: An integration injects the authenticated identity after login, scopes the tool's service account to the caller's tenant, and passes an account reference rather than the account's sensitive fields into the context.
3.2.guidance: Filter fields by necessity — if the language task does not need the value, a reference identifier usually suffices, because sensitive values in the context land in your request logs. One shared key across tenants makes a rate-limit breach unattributable, and an agent action with no audit record is increasingly treated as an action that cannot be permitted.

3.3.explanation: Accuracy-latency trade-offs are justified per configuration decision: the quality the stage requires, the latency the user or workflow tolerates, and what the cheaper option gives up, with the worst case budgeted rather than the median. Reliability controls belong at specific layers — retries sit beside the call itself, circuit breakers guard the service boundary, and fallback routing belongs with orchestration.
3.3.example: A routing classifier uses a fast model under a strict per-call budget while the rare escalation path accepts a slower, stronger model — each choice defended by the stage's tolerance, and a slow downstream service is guarded by a breaker at its boundary instead of a retry loop that multiplies load.
3.3.guidance: Name the accuracy requirement and the latency budget separately, then show why the chosen configuration serves both. Misplaced reliability controls are the recurring wrong answer: a retry inside an orchestration loop turns one slow dependency into many simultaneous calls.

3.4.explanation: Observability at scale means instrumenting the whole path — model calls, retrieval, tools, queues, downstream services — so any request can be reconstructed afterwards. Agents need trajectory-level tracing because the trajectory is the control flow: most tooling was built to alert on endpoints, not on the path an agent took.
3.4.example: When extraction quality slides, per-stage traces show retrieval returning stale documents while the model stage performs identically to the evaluation snapshot — localizing the failure without replaying traffic.
3.4.guidance: Propagate one trace identifier across roles and services so a run reconstructs end to end, and log enough to answer both what the system did and why. Deferring observability until after launch fails security review as often as it fails debugging.

3.5.explanation: A RAG pipeline is designed from the corpus shape and the query pattern, and neither is portable between projects. Section-numbered corpora preserve structure and retrieve at the level that answers the question; long-form prose splits on meaning boundaries so each unit stands alone; homogeneous text takes uniform spans with overlap — each choice trading retrieval precision, per-request latency, and ingestion complexity.
3.5.example: A manuals corpus keeps its section structure so retrieval returns the procedure that answers the question, while an FAQ corpus uses uniform overlapping chunks — imposing the manuals approach on the FAQ would complicate ingestion for no gain.
3.5.guidance: Design ingestion around what parses reliably, not what looks elegant — structure that must parse but cannot is a production failure. Add metadata and freshness controls for anything that changes, and name the trade you made among precision, latency, and upkeep.

3.6.explanation: Retrieval strategy matches the query pattern: keyword matching when queries hinge on identifiers, codes, or citations, semantic matching when queries are phrased differently from the source, and both run together with a standard rank-fusion rule when both kinds arrive — which is the usual case. Retrieval is for knowledge that holds still; anything whose current value is owned by another system needs a tool call to the system of record.
3.6.example: A policy assistant runs keyword and semantic search and merges the rankings, because engineers query by clause number while executives paraphrase — and account balances are answered by a tool call, never the index.
3.6.guidance: Recognize retrieval applied to live state by its symptoms: answers contradicting the database, results that shift with each refresh, staleness no embedding upgrade repairs. Match the strategy to observed queries, not to the last project.

3.7.explanation: Protocol choice turns on reuse, not familiarity: a direct API call or SDK when one product owns the integration, a shared tool protocol such as MCP when the same tool surface must be reachable from more than one client, a managed agent runtime when the model must iterate over tools inside your application, and a coding-agent entry point only when the user is an engineer working in a repository. Every deployment also separates three layers — entry point, build-time interface, and delivery route — each negotiated with a different stakeholder.
3.7.example: One internal tool surfaced to both a Claude Code deployment and a support agent justifies an MCP server; the same surface behind exactly one client buys the integration cost and none of the reuse.
3.7.guidance: Work down the list and stop at the first fit, and name which layer the question is actually about before recommending anything. When a stem names a regulation or an approved-vendor constraint, the discriminator is usually that one option was already ruled out.

3.8.explanation: Progressive discovery stages what the model can see and reach instead of loading a monolithic tool catalog or preloaded corpus, which costs tokens on every request, degrades selection accuracy as the catalog grows, and enlarges the space of actions never tested. The next step pulls what it needs.
3.8.example: An agent starts with a search tool and loads a domain's detailed tools only when work enters that domain, so per-request tokens stay flat and the tested action space stays bounded as coverage grows.
3.8.guidance: The monolithic strategy fails visibly as catalogs grow — selection accuracy falls before the cost does. Stage capability by the work in front of the agent, and let retrieval or an index step fetch the rest.

4.1.explanation: Evaluation metrics cover task quality, safety, security, latency, reliability, and cost, and each metric names the decision it informs. Turning a business requirement into a threshold means naming the specific behavior, setting the passing number from the requirement rather than from whatever the prototype scored, and enumerating the failure modes as dataset categories.
4.1.example: A vague accuracy goal becomes a grounded-fact rate at or above the agreed threshold on the labeled set, p95 latency under the published budget, and zero prohibited-content passes — each tied to a launch, routing, or rollback decision.
4.1.guidance: A metric you cannot connect to a decision is telemetry, not evaluation. Thresholds inherited from prototype scores measure the prototype, not the requirement.

4.2.explanation: Datasets mix curated cases, production samples, edge and adversarial inputs, and regression sets, while grading climbs a ladder: code-based checks for anything unambiguous, model-based judges for interpretation, human review for high-stakes or novel behavior and for calibrating the judge itself. Two rules make the ladder work — grade with a model other than the one tested, and prefer breadth, because many cheap automatically graded cases catch more regressions than a handful of meticulous ones.
4.2.example: A summarization suite grades schema and length in code, scores faithfulness with a judge calibrated on human-labeled samples, routes novel high-stakes cases to people, and updates whenever the prompt, retrieval strategy, or model changes.
4.2.guidance: Stakes decide how much you care; ambiguity decides the method — whether a prohibited action occurred is binary even when stakes are high. A stale suite is worse than none, and single-turn sets say nothing about conversation: multi-turn behavior needs its own dataset of full transcripts.

4.3.explanation: A believable experiment fixes four elements before the run: a falsifiable hypothesis naming treatment, expected direction, and constraints on secondary metrics; random assignment consistent per user or session; one primary metric chosen in advance; and a sample size computed from the effect to detect — model outputs vary more than deterministic systems, so the required sample is larger than intuition suggests. Shadow testing substitutes when exposure is unacceptable: run the candidate on copied traffic, serve everyone the current version, score offline.
4.3.example: A prompt change runs as an A/B split with per-session assignment and grounding rate declared as the primary metric; a regulated deployment instead shadows the candidate before anyone is exposed, accepting the loss of downstream behavioral signal.
4.3.guidance: Statistical and practical significance are different questions, and a primary-metric win that degrades cost or latency may not be a win at all. Watch interaction effects — a change that helps typical inputs can hurt a rare edge case that is common during a seasonal peak.

4.4.explanation: Four failure classes separate cleanly, and the fix lives where the failure lives: prompt failure (an ambiguous instruction the model filled its own way — fix the prompt), hallucination (fluent content with no basis in input or sources — fix grounding through retrieval, tools, or verification, because stronger wording cannot), model mismatch (the tier does not fit the work or changed unmeasured — re-select, gated by evaluation), and orchestration failure (a subagent dropped work or a coordinator lost its thread — fix failure boundaries and tracing).
4.4.example: A support bot invents return policies: the trace shows retrieval returning nothing while the model answered anyway — a grounding failure, so the fix is a tool or retrieval change, not a stronger instruction.
4.4.guidance: Attribute before acting: model drift (behavior changed on stable inputs), data drift (the input distribution changed), and a model update (the version changed underneath you) look similar and take different fixes. Read the trace first.

4.5.explanation: Optimization targets the tail, not the average: median latency does not breach service levels, token distributions are usually skewed so a cost model built on an average can understate spend by a wide margin, and aggregate dashboards look healthy while a small share of requests consumes most of the budget. The levers are model selection, prompt and context size, number of tool calls, and streaming versus batch.
4.5.example: A cost spike traces to one request category whose retrieved context tripled after a corpus change — visible only when spend is decomposed per request instead of averaged.
4.5.guidance: Decompose per-request cost and latency alongside the aggregate view, and fix the lever the decomposition points to. Sizing the cost model on the input distribution's heavy tail is what keeps the invoice a surprise-free document.

4.6.explanation: Monitoring pairs collection with a feedback loop — signals, triage, decision, action, review — recorded as a table before launch: every signal paired with the condition that fires it, the person who acts, and the action expected. Scheduled reviews fire on a cadence whether or not anything looks wrong, because residency confirmations and output audits are not threshold events.
4.6.example: A deployment pairs grounding-rate drift with a weekly owner review and a hard alert on error rate, so slow decay is caught by the cadence even when no threshold ever trips.
4.6.guidance: The characteristic failure is a metric drifting for weeks and surfacing as a stakeholder saying the output feels less useful — every signal collected, nothing mapped to a trigger. Build the loop at design time; retrofitting it costs far more.

5.1.explanation: Guardrails layer four covers, each covering what the one below cannot: trained behavior (broad harm classes on every request, blind to your policy), system instructions (role and constraints inside one request, talkable out of), screening (disallowed content in and out, blind to side-effecting actions), and action authorization (whether this caller may take this action now). The three control points answer three different questions — does the request reach the model, does the response reach the user, may the side-effecting call run.
5.1.example: An agent pairs input screening for hostile content, deterministic authorization scoped by role, and output screening for sensitive fields — because instructions alone are not enforcement, and one filter at the far end covers one point while sitting downstream of the irreversible step.
5.1.guidance: Choose the check type by the question: fuzzy intent needs a model-based classifier, crisp rules belong in deterministic code, and authorization should be deterministic almost without exception — an allowlist plus identity and scope, because it must be provable and replayable. Choose the failure direction deliberately: where an unscreened request would cause harm, fail closed.

5.2.explanation: The risk categories are direct prompt injection (overrides instructions from user input), indirect injection (arrives through retrieved documents and tool results the model treats as trustworthy — the dominant vector wherever retrieval or tools exist, and invisible to input screening), token-budget exhaustion, tool and action abuse, and data exposure into context or logs. Walk the request path and the data path together, naming the control at every entry point.
5.2.example: A retrieval agent's dominant risk is hostile instructions inside fetched documents — so documents are fenced and marked as data, consequential actions are gated regardless of content, and sensitive fields never enter the context window or the logs.
5.2.guidance: The most dangerous failure is quiet: a rule everybody believes is being enforced that exists in no layer at all — nothing can enforce a policy it was never handed. Screening covers content, never actions; authorization covers actions, never content quality.

5.3.explanation: Human review is routed by stakes, and stakes are two independent things: how easily a mistake can be undone and what it costs when it is not. Confidence decides how much volume can pass unsampled, and it is only useful to the degree it is calibrated. Placement trades coverage against latency — approval before the action buys no irreversible mistakes at the price of reviewer availability; audit after keeps throughput but only suits reversible decisions; sampling monitors without slowing the flow.
5.3.example: Refunds above a threshold require approval with the inputs, the draft, and the flagging reason attached; low-value routings are sampled for quality rather than held — and the review packet is what keeps the approval from becoming rubber-stamping.
5.3.guidance: Two failures collapse review into theater: volume beyond what a person can read produces consent fatigue, and a bare output with a single approve button leaves nothing to weigh. Concentrate review where it carries information — approving a plan or handling an exception — rather than signing every step.

5.4.explanation: Each obligation — GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP — becomes a control, an owner, and living evidence, because regulations state outcomes and leave the implementation to you. Choosing a compliant delivery route is a prerequisite, not proof: a reviewer accepts a countersigned agreement, a screenshot of the live setting, an authorization record, or a query returning the expected rows — a design document is none of these.
5.4.example: A regulated deployment maps its data-handling obligation to the field-minimization filter, its retention obligation to the log lifecycle, and its access obligation to the authorization record — each with a named owner and an artifact that demonstrates it is operating.
5.4.guidance: A control with no named owner and no living artifact stops operating quietly, and the gap turns up in an audit instead of a design review — the costliest possible place. Revalidate the register on a cadence, because configurations drift after sign-off.

5.5.explanation: Unequal outcomes enter at points you own: a retrieval corpus that over- or under-represents groups, prompt framing that encodes an assumption, few-shot examples carrying the same skew, and downstream routing that sends some groups along different paths — and an aggregate outcome metric can look healthy while harm concentrates in one subgroup. Transparency serves three readers from the same decision-level log: the affected person needs inputs and reason phrased so they can act, the regulator needs evidence comparable cases were treated comparably, the team needs the full trace.
5.5.example: An underwriting assistant's aggregate approval rate looks healthy while one subgroup is routed to manual review more often — visible only when outcomes are segmented by group.
5.5.guidance: Instrument fairness at the four entry points rather than assuming the model arrives fair. Keep the decision log minimal, retention-bounded, and access-controlled — it falls inside the compliance register too.

6.1.explanation: Discovery is structured elicitation, not conversation: listen to the goal in the stakeholder's own business language, translate it into requirements and named assumptions, and write both down before moving on. Experience words — seamless, fast, simple, intuitive — are signals that more questions are needed, never requirements themselves. Every statement is forced through four categories: what the system must do, must not do, must cost, and must prove.
6.1.example: A request for a seamless handoff to agents resolves into a latency target, an integration boundary, a rule for how work passes to a person, and a failure state that exposes nothing — each buildable and measurable, with the prohibited actions captured because nobody volunteers them unprompted.
6.1.guidance: Record one row per item: the stakeholder's words, the constraint underneath, the design decision it compels, and what you are still assuming. Do not sketch architecture mid-call — the sketch's plausibility is what stops the questions, because a stakeholder who sees a confident design assumes the questions were asked.

6.2.explanation: A trade-off is presented in three elements: the benefit, the concession, and the price of undoing the choice after the rest of the system has been built on top of it — adding its effect on compliance posture in regulated settings. The package travels upward as the options considered, the criteria weighed, the recommendation, and the risks that survive it.
6.2.example: Recommending retrieval over fine-tuning names the quality gain, the operating cost, and what unwinding would take once ingestion, caching, and evaluation are built — the third element usually decides the room, because it converts a technical comparison into a business one.
6.2.guidance: Open on the business consequence instead of the design, and state the limits plainly — naming them is what earns a security reviewer's confidence. Approving a choice without understanding the unwind cost is not an informed decision, and the stakeholder will say so when the invoice arrives.

6.3.explanation: Observability collects signals; a feedback loop decides what they mean — signals, triage, decision, action, review, existing as a table before launch that pairs every signal with the condition that fires it, the person who acts, and the action expected. Service levels must trace to a source: latency from the user-experience expectation captured in discovery, availability from business centrality, quality from the evaluation acceptance criteria.
6.3.example: A handoff table pairs grounding-rate drift with a weekly owner review and a hard error-rate alert, includes a quarterly residency confirmation that fires on schedule rather than on threshold, and gives the sponsor a consumption forecast before the first invoice.
6.3.guidance: A number that traces to none of these sources is a target someone found reasonable. Cost is the expectation that most often fails to survive launch — production volume routinely runs far above the pilot, so deliver the forecast and the spend-control posture early.

6.4.explanation: Documentation serves three readers at once: the engineer inheriting the system needs decisions, rejected alternatives, and the trade-off each rejection settled; the compliance reviewer needs each obligation paired with its control, owner, and evidence artifact; the returning architect needs dated decisions with assumptions marked as assumptions. The completeness test is practical — could an equally capable architect who missed every design session change this system safely on the document alone?
6.4.example: A decision record captures the choice and its date, the options considered and not chosen, the gain and cost and reversal price of the trade-off, the owner going forward, the evidence artifact, and whether that evidence is current.
6.4.guidance: A diagram records the shape of the system, not the rationale — without rejected alternatives a successor cannot tell which choices carry weight and which were preference, and will overturn a sound one for a reason that looks sound at the time. Assumptions recorded as assumptions return as questions; assumptions woven in as facts return as incidents.

6.5.explanation: The lifecycle runs discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration, and knowing which phase a decision belongs to is what tells you when a phase can close. When a deployment spans more than one route or entry point, write down which surface owns which task before integration begins, or routing drifts and a surface chosen for one job quietly acquires another.
6.5.example: At a handoff gate the items that belong are runbooks, owners, service levels, and monitoring scope — a proposal for new model evaluation belongs to design, however sound it would be there, and recognizing that is the discriminating skill.
6.5.guidance: Learn the phases as an ordering, not only a list: read the stem for the phase marker and reject any option that belongs to a later phase no matter how sound. Close with an outcome document — use case, scope boundary, the business metric before, the same metric after, the control that makes the comparison checkable — and capture the before number at the start, because it cannot be reconstructed at the end.

7.1.explanation: Team configuration separates what shapes the agent — standing project instructions, packaged procedures, scoped subagents, connected tool servers — from what governs it: lifecycle hooks, permission modes, approval flows, and sandboxing. A guarantee that must hold has to come from code and configuration, not from wording in an instructions file.
7.1.example: A team ships one shared baseline — agreed project instructions, a reviewed tool set, one permission posture — so configuration is reviewed and improved once instead of drifting across individual setups, with spend guardrails set deliberately: default model, allowed models, effort guidance, per-user and rate caps.
7.1.guidance: Choose the distribution mechanism by reach against governance: organization-wide availability reaches everyone with the least version control, group-scoped packages carry versioned updates and rollback, repository-scoped artifacts version alongside the code, and programmatic reuse pins an explicit version. Unmanaged model choice compounds across every teammate and request.

7.2.explanation: Assistance pays off where the work already happens — while code is being written, during review, inside the test cycle — rather than in a chat tab someone visits occasionally. Each stage keeps the discipline it always needed: whoever ships generated code must be able to explain it, a flagged finding is an input to judgment rather than a verdict, and a proposed diagnosis is checked against evidence before anyone acts on it.
7.2.example: A team pairs code generation with an explicit verification checklist covering correctness, security, maintainability, and human understanding, then automates the gate so it fires on every change instead of relying on a reviewer's attention.
7.2.guidance: Engineer adoption rather than announcing it: enable one champion per team, let them convert a real workflow and absorb the early friction, then seed in batches. The two named failure modes are lumpy adoption — heavy use by a few that never standardizes — and stalling at basic chat, where access never becomes repository-aware work.

7.3.explanation: Support means translating symptoms into causes, then handing the path over. Quality that slid without a deployment points at a changed model or prompt, or an index drifting as the corpus grew — re-run the evaluation set and diff what moved. Response times that jumped point at context growth, a slowed dependency, or cached prefixes that stopped matching — trace the slowest span and read per-request token counts and cache hits. Intermittent tool failures point at credentials, throttling, or an unhandled error path. Spend rising against flat usage points at requests drifting to a costlier tier or caching quietly regressing.
7.3.example: A gradual quality slide with no deployment is diagnosed by re-running the evaluation suite and diffing results against the model version change — then the runbook records the symptom-to-action path so the team handles it without you.
7.3.guidance: Resolving one incident yourself is firefighting; leave behind a runbook of known symptom-to-action paths and an escalation map naming who owns what. Instrument token usage, latency, and error rate per call from the start, so a spike becomes a row you can sort instead of a mystery on the invoice.
